reason: Under 'Differences between SCPs and RCPs' the two quotes state verbatim that SCPs are principal-centric and limit maximum permissions of principals in member accounts, and RCPs are resource-centric and limit maximum permissions for resources in member accounts.
Quote under 'Using SCPs and RCPs' says they are independent controls, you can enable only SCPs or RCPs or both, and both together create a data perimeter around identities and resources.
Under 'Testing effects of SCPs' AWS strongly recommends not attaching SCPs to the root without thorough testing, and instead creating an OU to move accounts into one at a time or in small numbers.
Under 'SCP effects on permissions': users and roles must still be granted IAM permission policies; a user without any has no access even if the applicable SCPs allow all services and actions.

Under 'Security Tooling (Audit) account' the quotes state centralized delegated admin access to security tooling, view-only investigative access into all accounts, and that it is an aggregation point for the listed services (claim lists a subset with 'such as').

Under 'Constrain access to sensitive data' the quote states limiting sensitive data stores to dedicated accounts tightens access control and lets you restrict permissions at the coarse-grained account level rather than fine-grained access in one broad account.

Quote says separate non-production and production accounts by default separate the resources and data of a workload environment; the surrounding paragraph under 'Apply distinct security controls by environment' gives the different security and operational controls purpose.

Quote recommends a single organization managing all accounts and says an organization is a security boundary that maintains consistency across accounts; context adds central application of policies and service-level configurations.

First quote: programmatic account creation via CLI, SDKs or APIs and central provisioning with CloudFormation StackSets; second quote: separate groups for development and production accounts provisioned with StackSets.
Quote: a tag policy can specify enforcement of noncompliant tagging operations on specified resource types, so noncompliant requests on those types are prevented from completing; condition matches.
Quotes state tag policies standardize tags on resources in the organization's accounts and that untagged resources or tags not defined in the policy are not evaluated for compliance.

The row supports 50 tags per root, OU or account, but the section 'Maximum and minimum values' calls these the default maximums and says increases can be requested for some values; nothing states this one is non-adjustable, so default_or_max=max with adjustable=false says more than the quote.

Quote: trusted access lets the trusted service perform tasks in the organization and its accounts on your behalf, does not otherwise affect user or role permissions, and the service can create a service-linked role in accounts when needed.

SEC01-BP02 quotes: root user is the most privileged user and in some cases cannot be constrained by security policies; prioritize the management account root user, and preventative controls can be placed on member account root users.

Note on the RCP page states verbatim: use an SCP to limit permissions of IAM principals within member accounts; use an RCP to restrict external IAM principals requesting access to resources in member accounts.

Default loss of access is quoted, but the exception drops its condition: the quote limits RetainSharingOnAccountLeaveOrganization to account-to-account sharing within the organization (context: does not apply to OUs or the entire organization), while the claim makes it a general exception for any share.

Quotes state random mapping of physical AZs to names per account (us-east-1a may differ), an AZ ID like use1-az1 is the same physical location in every account, and a subnet shared in use1-az2 is available in the consumer AZ whose AZ ID is also use1-az2.
Quote: only your own organization and its OUs can be added; OUs or organizations from outside cannot; outside principals can be individual accounts or, for supported services, IAM roles and users.
Doc history row dated April 19, 2023: added support for customer managed permission in the RAM console, to author and maintain fine-grained resource access controls for supported resource types.
Doc history row dated August 20, 2026: you can now share Amazon EBS volumes with other AWS accounts or your organization.
Doc history row dated September 24, 2026: you can now share EventBridge custom event buses with other AWS accounts, or with IAM roles and users, using AWS RAM.

Doc history row supports the June 8, 2023 increase from 20 to 250 pending invitations per sharing account, but the qualifier condition 'sharing with accounts outside the organization' is not in this quote or its context.
Doc history row dated October 30, 2024: you can now share Amazon VPC Security groups with other AWS accounts or within your organization.
Doc history row dated March 31, 2023: you can now share Amazon VPC Lattice service and service network resources with other AWS accounts.
Under 'How resource sharing works': sharing grants access for principals in the consuming account, and policies and permissions applying to its roles and users also apply to the shared resource.

The row under 'Default limit' supports 1,500 customer managed permissions as a default, but adjustable=true is not established for this quota: the page intro says only that you can request an increase for some of these limits, without naming this one.
Important note states disabling trusted access to AWS Organizations removes principals within the organization from all resource shares and they lose access to those shared resources.

Quotes: you must enable sharing via the RAM console or enable-sharing-with-aws-organization (context: ensures the service-linked role is created); enabling trusted access from the Organizations console or enable-aws-service-access does not create the role and you can't share within the organization.
FAQ quote: AWS managed permissions are created and maintained by AWS, and every resource type has a default AWS managed permission.
FAQ quote: you can specify IAM policies to control access to resources shared with you.
FAQ quote limits sharing with IAM roles and IAM users to supported resource types ('For supported resource types, you can also share ... with IAM roles and IAM users').
FAQ quote: all RAM API calls are logged in CloudTrail, and CloudWatch Events are triggered whenever resource shares change.
Under Billing, the question about charges for sharing is answered: no, you can share resources at no additional cost.

FAQ quote: a managed permission defines actions, conditions and principals for supported resource types in a share, and you associate either an AWS managed or a customer managed permission with each resource type.
FAQ quote lists the steps: add resources to a resource share, choose a managed permission per resource type, and specify who gets access.
FAQ quote: you can share with any AWS account, and with OUs or the entire organization when you are in an organization and sharing within it is enabled.
FAQ quote: shared resources appear in the respective resource console pages and List/Describe APIs; the Route 53 Resolver example in context shows them alongside the account's own resources.
FAQ quote: you can stop sharing a resource by removing it from the resource share or by deleting the resource share.

Under 'How managed permissions work': after the share is created RAM uses the managed permission to generate a resource-based policy attached to each shared resource; for a managed permission the effect is always Allow.

Quotes: two types of managed permissions; one default AWS managed permission for every supported resource type; customer managed permissions you author and maintain, with context tying them to least privilege.
